title: Looking back: renewal and today
hook: reform, peaceful protest, 1947, 1984, and the Sikhs of every continent

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at kingdom and loss, and your line was lost and kept. What did you notice that stayed? Today, the last stretch of the long story, the one still being written. Day one thousand sixty.

Near the close of the Ardas, wherever it's said, come two words. Chardi kala. Rising spirits, high spirits, a spirit that keeps climbing. Sikhs say it in a gurdwara in Amritsar, in a living room in a cold country, beside a hospital bed, at a wedding. After the kingdom was gone, the Sikh story could have shrunk to a memory. It didn't. It renewed itself, suffered again, and spread far from Punjab. Today, looking back at renewal and today.
screen: `NEAR THE ARDAS'S CLOSE: CHARDI KALA.` → `SAID WHEREVER THE ARDAS IS SAID.` → `THE STORY DIDN'T SHRINK.`

segments.voice: First, renewal. Reformers rose: Baba Dayal calling Sikhs back to the formless God, the Namdharis in white, and the Singh Sabhas founding schools, presses and study circles to renew Sikh learning. Second, peaceful protest. When Sikhs set out to free their gurdwaras from the mahants, hereditary custodians the reformers accused of misrule, protesters pledged not to strike back, and took the blows. Nankana remembers peaceful martyrs. Later came a long campaign for a Punjabi-speaking state. Third, the wounds. Partition split Punjab. Villages burned, trains of refugees crossed the new border, violence struck on every side, and Guru Nanak's birthplace was left on the far side of the line. Families started again from nothing. And then what Sikhs simply call 1984: the army's assault on the Harmandir complex, and the killings of Sikhs in Delhi and other cities that followed. It is still a wound, still remembered with care. Fourth, today. Sikhs now live far from Punjab, in many countries, building gurdwaras, opening langars to whoever walks in, serving in disasters with food and water. And right after chardi kala, the Ardas ends with one more phrase: sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not of Sikhs alone. Of everyone. That's where the long story stands now: renewed, wounded, and spread out, still asking for the good of all. Today's line: everywhere, still rising.
screen: `RENEWAL: REFORMERS AND SCHOOLS.` · `PEACEFUL PROTEST: BLOWS NOT RETURNED.` · `THE WOUNDS: PARTITION AND 1984.` · `TODAY: FAR FROM PUNJAB, SERVING ALL.` · then, large: `EVERYWHERE, STILL RISING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for Sikhs everywhere. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind the places from today: Amritsar, Nankana, a village rebuilt, a gurdwara in a city far away, a volunteer handing out food after a storm. If you pray, you can pray for Sikhs everywhere, for their safety and their chardi kala, and you can hold the Ardas's last wish with them, sarbat da bhala, the good of all. If you don't pray, simply wish them well, one place at a time, on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Today at the reformers, the peaceful protesters, the wounds of Partition and 1984, and the Sikhs who now live far from Punjab, still saying chardi kala. Today's word.
Your line: everywhere, still rising. Today, if you pass a gurdwara or meet a Sikh neighbor, a classmate or a coworker, let the whole long story stand behind them for a moment. Day one thousand sixty.

howItsDone: The Ardas closes by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, through the Name, and sarbat da bhala, the good of all; Sikhs in Punjab and far beyond say it at the end of prayers and gatherings, and remember Partition and 1984 in gatherings each year.

options: a curse on those who hurt you.
rising spirits, and the good of all.

fork.reveal: the Ardas ends with chardi kala and sarbat da bhala: rising spirits, and the good of all.

original.note: chardi kala, rising spirits: the hope Sikhs name at the close of the Ardas.

trapdoor: what you thought: modern history is just a list of hard events.
what it means: renewal, peaceful protest, deep wounds, and a people spread far from Punjab, still in chardi kala.
what a scholar hears: the Ardas's closing asks for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala together, rising spirits joined to the good of all, not of Sikhs alone.
